extracted.intended_audience: nonprofits, individual citizens, advocacy groups, policy advocates, and subject-matter experts who want to submit effective public comments on U.S. federal rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and submitting public comments under the Administrative Procedure Act to influence U.S. federal rulemaking. Covers when to engage, what kinds of content agencies find useful, and practical tactics to increase noticeability and legal usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the rulemaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: Know that federal agencies write rules to implement laws passed by Congress and that the notice-and-comment rulemaking process under the Administrative Procedure Act is the primary mechanism for public input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the legal and procedural context helps set realistic goals for influence and clarifies how comments become part of the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus where you have specific expertise or experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose to comment on rules where you or your organization have particular technical knowledge, lived experience, or subject-matter expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments grounded in expertise are more likely to introduce new, credible information the agency can use; avoid commenting on every rule broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target rules with high economic or social stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize rulemakings where the economic or social consequences are large relative to the effort of commenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-stakes rules are more likely to attract agency attention and justify investing resources in a substantive, well-documented comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage where the agency has discretion to act
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer rulemakings where agencies exercise policy judgment or have discretion such that reasoned comments can shape outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency's hands are largely tied by statute, comments are less likely to change substantive outcomes; focus on areas with regulatory latitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize timing and pre-proposal opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of when pre-proposal influence opportunities have closed and whether comment is your primary chance to affect the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit early if possible; if pre-proposal windows remain, engage there for greater influence. Late comments are less able to shape agency thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame comments to be useful to agency staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Write comments that help overburdened agency staff quickly understand actionable information about implementation, costs, stakeholders, and alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies have time/resource constraints—concise, well-structured comments that surface problems and solutions are more usable than broad statements of support or opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe real-world implementation problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the proposed rule would work in practice and identify concrete implementation issues the agency may have overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specifics about how rules would affect operations, compliance pathways, timing, or enforcement to make your critique practical and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify affected stakeholders the agency may not have engaged
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out groups, sectors, or communities the agency might have missed when assessing impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming and describing unengaged stakeholders helps agencies broaden their analysis and may reveal uncovered costs or benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide cost or burden estimates with verifiable assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticizing regulatory impacts, include quantitative estimates of costs or burdens and make the assumptions transparent and verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies value estimates they can trace and check; vague or unsupported cost claims are less persuasive than numbers with citations and clear methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose alternative regulatory approaches and tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer feasible alternative rules or regulatory designs and clearly explain their tradeoffs relative to the proposed option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that merely complain are weak; actionable alternatives (with analysis of benefits, costs, and practical steps) are far more useful to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with the agency's regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Interact substantively with the agency's cost-benefit analysis and other analytic materials rather than ignoring them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies often follow EO 12866 requirements—comments should address assumptions, methods, and omissions in that analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge specific analytic assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Question concrete assumptions the agency used (e.g., discount rates, valuation of a statistical life) when they seem inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing to particular parameter choices and explaining why they are wrong (with evidence or alternative values) is more persuasive than generic critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide better data or evidence than the agency has
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit new empirical information, studies, or datasets that improve on what the agency used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality primary data or peer-reviewed studies can correct agency errors or fill analytical gaps; include citations and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify costs or benefits the agency missed
rubrics_metrics.description: Help the agency recognize impacts omitted from its analysis, including indirect or distributional effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify why omitted items matter to the overall assessment and, where possible, quantify them or provide sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with the alternatives the agency considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on the set of alternatives in the regulatory analysis—whether they are adequate and whether important options were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain which alternatives should be added or modified and why, including implications for costs, benefits, and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite specific provisions and docket identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference exact section and paragraph numbers from the Federal Register notice and include the docket ID in your submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific citations make comments easier to process and tie critique to the precise regulatory text the agency is considering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the limits: agencies don't tally support/opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that agencies generally do not treat the number of supportive or opposing comments as a simple vote count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The content and quality of comments matter more than raw tallies; campaigns that rely only on volume are less likely to change analytic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that a 'vote' is not the goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid thinking of comments primarily as a way to register a vote for or against the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive, evidence-based comments are the pathway to influence; pure expressions of support or opposition are legally and analytically weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure comments are on the rulemaking record for legal challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: If your goal includes preserving legal arguments for later judicial review, make sure those arguments are presented in comments on the administrative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often require issues to have been raised during notice-and-comment to be reviewable; include clear, on-record legal and factual claims you may later rely on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mass campaigns for political signaling, not substantive influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that mass comment drives are can signal public sentiment but rarely provide the detailed, novel information agencies need to change rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine grassroots mobilization with a smaller number of technical, well-documented comments to maximize both political and analytic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make comments findable: clear subject line and docket ID
rubrics_metrics.description: Format and label your submission so agency staff can locate it quickly (include a clear subject line and the docket ID).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative staff triage large comment volumes; discoverability increases the chance your content will be read and cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make comments useful: give information the agency can use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize actionable information—data, concrete examples, and specific critiques—over broad expressions of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful comments shorten staff work by supplying evidence and reasoning they can incorporate into the final rule or respond to directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make claims referencable: include citations and specific claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Support assertions with citations, data sources, and clearly stated claims so agency staff can reference them in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencable comments are more likely to be discussed in agency responses and to survive legal scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal stories with specific facts
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonprofits and individuals, personal narratives anchored with concrete facts are more persuasive than generic expressions of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity about harms, times, places, and effects makes testimonial evidence actionable and credible to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate technical and grassroots efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine detailed technical comments from experts with grassroots engagement to provide both substantive analysis and political visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination leverages strengths of different participants—experts supply analytic weight while grassroots demonstrate affected constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit early in the comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: File comments early, before opposition organizes and while agencies are still shaping analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early submissions can influence subsequent stakeholder framing and agency revisions; late comments have less chance to change core analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track agency responses in the final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor the agency's final rule and its response to comments to see how your input was used or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracking responses informs future strategy, helps identify analytic gaps, and is necessary if you plan further advocacy or litigation.
